newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - Gloomy gilts penned in on all sides.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - Gloomy gilts penned in on all sides.

text.p: British gilts may get a brief lift from news on Wednesday that monetary policy was left on hold, but a painful tightening has only been postponed for a month or two, analysts said.

With the threat of interest rate rises early in the new year and a widening political cleft over Britain's future in Europe and stance on a single currency, gilts will remain pretty gloomy until the spring of 1997.
"There are dual forces at work in the gilt market," said Adrian Owens, economist at Julius Baer Investments in London.
"At current yield levels gilts are attractive, especially given the currency background, but the big concern is that we are in an environment in which interest rates are going up."
The Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke left monetary policy unchanged after his monthly meeting with the Bank of England on Wednesday -- a move widely expected.
But analysts said any relief for gilts, which have been outclassed consistently in recent months by debt markets in Sweden, Spain and Italy, would be barely noticeable.
"Everything points in the direction of underperformance by gilts," said Adam Cole, UK economist at HSBC James Capel in London. "We're bulls on growth and bears on inflation."
Analysts said a number of worries would continue to dog the market for now, although Owens and Joanne Collins of Nomura said the spring of 1997 may bring a little more joy.

Inflation, which leapt to 3.3 percent in October, is likely to remain the same for November, according to a Reuters poll of economists. That will do little to ease the pressure on Clarke to tighten monetary policy in the new year, analysts said.
With a general election looming by May and a government fighting over policy on European monetary union and wheezing to stay in power, the political backdrop is of little help.
But Collins, a senior economist at Nomura in London, said gilts should start to pick up in the longer term.

Noting the dwindling yields offered in what used to be classed as the world's high-yield markets such as Italy, Sweden, Austrlia, and Spain, she said investors will begin to see gilts as an attractive alternative.
"We're running out of options for high-yield markets," she said. "Gilts will start to look pretty good in the medium term, particularly once we get over the hurdle of the election."

Owens said investors may even be lured back in the run-up to the election, betting that a victory by the left-wing Labour Party would put Britain into a more euro-friendly position, increasing the chance that EMU convergence will show through in the gilt/Bund 10-year yield spread.
"I would be increasingly optimistic as we head towards the election," Owens said. "People will start buying ahead of a Labour result and a more pro-European government."
Taking a three to four month view, Owens said the gilt/Bund gap could slim from its current 184 basis points to around the 165 level as gilts outperform.
